questions.q: What is a realistic target size for a capstone SFT dataset, and what matters more than volume?
options: Millions of examples; volume is the only thing that matters
A few hundred to a couple thousand well-chosen examples, where quality and style consistency matter far more than raw volume
Exactly 50 examples, since more would overfit any model
There is no practical upper or lower bound worth considering
questions.explain: The lesson states a few hundred to a couple thousand well-chosen examples is a realistic and sufficient target for a capstone, with quality and consistency of style mattering far more than raw volume.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend using the model's actual apply_chat_template rather than a hand-rolled formatting approach?
options: Because apply_chat_template is purely cosmetic and has no effect on training quality
Because a hand-rolled template that is close-but-not-quite what the model expects is a common, hard-to-spot source of poor fine-tuning results
Because hand-rolled templates are always faster to execute at training time
Because apply_chat_template is required only for base models, never for instruction-tuned ones
questions.explain: Using the tokenizer's own apply_chat_template, loaded from the exact chosen model, avoids subtle formatting mismatches that a hand-rolled approximation can introduce and that are difficult to diagnose later.

questions.q: What is the purpose of prompt masking during SFT dataset preparation?
options: To hide the dataset from other team members for privacy reasons
To ensure loss is computed only on response tokens, not on the prompt tokens, during training
To remove all prompts from the dataset before training begins
To encrypt the dataset before uploading it to the Hub
questions.explain: Prompt masking, as covered in the SFT chapter, ensures the model is trained to predict responses rather than being penalized or rewarded for reproducing the prompt tokens themselves.

questions.q: Why is a deduplication pass recommended before training, especially when examples are partly model-generated?
options: Because duplicate examples cause training to crash with an error
Because near-duplicate examples inflate the effective weight of a handful of patterns in a small dataset, skewing what the model learns
Because deduplication is required by the Hugging Face Hub's terms of service
Because duplicates increase the parameter count of the model
questions.explain: Near-duplicate examples, common when drafts are generated by a model, effectively over-represent a handful of patterns relative to the rest of the dataset, which a simple dedup pass catches cheaply.

questions.q: Why must the held-out split be set aside before training and not examined again until the evaluation lesson?
options: Because held-out data is only used for data augmentation during training
Because looking at or training on the held-out data would make the later evaluation measure performance on data the model has already seen, rather than genuine generalization
Because the held-out split is identical to the general-capability benchmark used for the forgetting check
Because held-out splits are only required when using full fine-tuning, not LoRA
questions.explain: A held-out split set aside before training, and left unexamined until final evaluation, is what allows measuring genuine task performance on data the model never saw, rather than quietly evaluating on already-seen examples.
